description: We are Paparajote lunar, a team of five from Murcia: environmental scientists and engineers. We are tackling the Harmonization of MODIS and VIIRS Hot Spots challenge: turning 20+ years of NASA FIRMS fire detections into one consistent record and a web app with a burning activity calendar, starting with the Iberian Peninsula and the Region of Murcia. Our team is complete.
summary:
Ctrl + Fire turns NASA's two active-fire records into one. MODIS (1 km, since 2000) and VIIRS (375 m, since 2012) cannot be put side by side: VIIRS detects several times more hotspots simply because it sees smaller fires, so a plain join makes fire look like it exploded in 2012.

Our open web app, live at https://paparajotelunar.com, harmonizes both into a single monthly record from July 2002 to today, for any place on Earth. For each country it learns how many hotspots VIIRS sees for each one Aqua MODIS sees (2012-2017), grades seven models on data they never saw (2018 to mid-2021), keeps the best one and rebuilds 2002-2011 on the VIIRS scale. Two of the models treat day and night passes separately, because the gap between the sensors is much larger at night.

Users pick a place by searching, tapping the map or drawing a shape, and get a burning calendar, how the current month compares with its historical median, the years ranked, a map that zooms from a 25 km harmonized grid down to the real 375 m detections, and CSV downloads. Every country shows its own test score, and estimated or provisional months are labelled as such.
details:
WHAT IT DOES

Ctrl + Fire is a web app that shows when and where fire burns, for any area on Earth, on one consistent record from July 2002 to today. It answers the question the challenge asks: is this month's fire normal for this place?

HOW IT WORKS

1. Ingest. The backend downloads every country file of the NASA FIRMS yearly archive (MODIS, Suomi NPP VIIRS and NOAA-20 VIIRS), keeps Aqua and VIIRS vegetation fires, and sums them per 0.25 degree cell and month. Recent days come from the FIRMS area API. It runs again every 6 hours.

2. Harmonize. Aqua MODIS and Suomi NPP VIIRS observed at the same local time until 2021, so they can be compared. For each country we learn their relationship on 2012-2017 and grade seven models on 2018 to mid-2021, data the models never saw: constant ratio, ratio by month, log-log regression, quantile mapping, a negative binomial count model, and day/night versions of two of them. The best one rebuilds 2002-2011 on the VIIRS scale. Countries with too little fire use a model pooled with their neighbours. One satellite per period, never added together: Aqua corrected until January 2012, Suomi NPP until 1 November 2026, NOAA-20 after Suomi NPP ended.

3. Serve. An open API returns the calendar of any area with medians, anomalies and ranked years, a map grid, the raw sensor comparison and CSV exports.

WHAT THE USER GETS

- Atlas: a map of the world's fire on one scale. Search a place, tap the map or draw an area, and a panel shows its hotspots since 2002, whether this month is normal, the last fire, the peak month and the usual fire season.

- Three map layers: harmonized hotspots per cell, unusual fire against each month's own history, and every single detection drawn at its real size (375 m for VIIRS, 1 km for MODIS).

- Compare: the same place in two periods, on two maps that move together and share one colour scale.

- Satellite imagery: NASA GIBS daily images under the data (true colour and shortwave-infrared composites that show burn scars).

- Calendar, anomalies, sensor comparison and CSV downloads for the chosen place, and a method page with each country's test results.

- Ask: Ember, an assistant that answers questions by querying our harmonized record through the same open API. It uses a generative language model, so its answers can contain mistakes; the page says so.

WHAT WE FOUND

- In Spain, raw MODIS undercounts VIIRS by about 86%; the chosen model is within about 9% on the test years, with a monthly R² of 0.87.

- In Spain, the step at the 2012 sensor change is ×5.87 in the raw record and ×0.99 after harmonizing; Aqua alone, which flew on both sides, gives ×1.00.

- VIIRS sees about 4 times more hotspots than MODIS by day and about 12 times more at night in Iberia; the same pattern holds in Greece, Chile and Malaysia.

- No single model wins everywhere, so each country is tested separately.

BENEFITS AND IMPACT

Emergency teams, land managers, scientists and journalists can compare fire activity before and after 2012 without mistaking a change of sensor for a real trend. Our local case is the Region of Murcia.

HONEST LIMITS

Months before February 2012 are estimates of what VIIRS would have seen: good for monthly patterns, not for single fires. A hotspot is one satellite detection, not one fire, and a month without hotspots is not proof of no fire. The latest months are provisional. Countries whose model passed the test less well are marked "review".

TOOLS

Study and proof of concept: Python (pandas, NumPy, statsmodels) in Google Colab, with automated tests. Backend: Go, PostgreSQL, Docker, Caddy. Frontend: React, TypeScript, Vite, Tailwind CSS, TanStack Query, Leaflet, d3-geo. GitHub Actions for tests and deployment. OpenAI API for the Ask assistant. The Go harmonization was checked value by value against the Python study.
